examples: The sun rises in the morning.
The rain stopped and the sun came out.
The sun is really bright today.
nuance: 해 means the sun in the sky and pairs with 뜨다 to rise and 지다 to set, so beginners use 해가 떠요 and 해가 져요 a lot. After bad weather, 해가 나다 means the sun comes out. It also stands for daytime sunshine in casual talk.
mistakes: Saying 해가 와요 instead of the correct 해가 떠요
Mixing up 해 the sun and 햇빛 sunlight as if they were the same word

examples: The sunshine is really warm today.
The sun was strong so I wore a hat.
I soaked up the sun at the park.
nuance: 햇볕 is the warm sunshine you feel on your skin, while 햇빛 is more the light you see, so 햇볕 goes with 따뜻하다 and 쬐다. Koreans say 햇볕을 쬐다 to mean basking in the sun. On a warm day 햇볕이 좋다 is common small talk.
mistakes: Writing 햇볕 with the wrong final consonant, as 햇볃 or 햇볓
Saying 햇볕을 봐요 when natural Korean is 햇볕을 쬐어요

examples: The sunset glow is really pretty in the evening.
I saw the sunset glow at the sea.
nuance: 노을 is the red and orange glow in the sky around sunset and uses the verb 지다, as in 노을이 지다. It is a favorite scene to watch and photograph in Korea. People often add 예쁘다 or 붉다 to describe how it looks.
mistakes: Saying 노을이 와요 instead of the natural 노을이 져요
Confusing 노을 sunset glow with 노른자 egg yolk because of the similar sound

examples: I cannot go outside because the storm is blowing.
The storm passed and the weather got nice.
nuance: 폭풍 is a strong storm with heavy wind and rain and pairs with 오다 to come or 불다 to blow. People say 폭풍이 심하다 when it is severe. Once it clears, 폭풍이 지나가다 means the storm has passed.
mistakes: Saying 폭풍이 해요 instead of 폭풍이 와요 or 폭풍이 불어요
Confusing 폭풍 storm with 폭염 heat wave

examples: I was startled because hail came.
The hail was really big today.
nuance: 우박 is hail, the small ice balls that fall from the sky, and it uses 내리다 to fall or casual 오다 to come. Beginners can say 우박이 내려요 just like 비가 와요. Because hail is sudden, 갑자기 우박이 오다 is a common phrase.
mistakes: Saying 우박이 불어요 with the wind verb instead of 우박이 내려요
Confusing 우박 hail with 소나기 a sudden rain shower

usage: I look at the full moon
examples: The full moon is really bright.
I looked at the full moon with my family.
nuance: 보름달 is the full round moon and uses 뜨다 to rise just like 해 and 달. Koreans watch the 보름달 on holidays like Chuseok and often make a wish. Describe it with 밝다 for bright or 둥글다 for round.
mistakes: Saying 보름달이 와요 instead of the correct 보름달이 떠요
Confusing 보름달 full moon with 초승달 crescent moon

usage: I look at the crescent moon
examples: A crescent moon rose in the sky.
The crescent moon is very thin.
The crescent moon is pretty today.
nuance: 초승달 is the thin crescent moon seen early in the lunar month and uses 뜨다 to rise. Its shape is described with 가늘다 thin or 예쁘다 pretty. It is the opposite of the round 보름달.
mistakes: Confusing 초승달 crescent moon with 보름달 full moon
Saying 초승달이 와요 instead of the natural 초승달이 떠요

examples: The starlight is bright in the night sky.
The starlight is really beautiful in the countryside.
nuance: 별빛 is the light of the stars and combines 별 star with 빛 light. It is described with 밝다 bright or 반짝이다 to twinkle. You see beautiful 별빛 far from city lights, so it often appears in poetic descriptions.
mistakes: Confusing 별빛 starlight with 달빛 moonlight
Saying 별빛이 와요 when light does not take the verb 오다

examples: I took a walk under the moonlight.
nuance: 달빛 is the light of the moon and combines 달 moon with 빛 light. It pairs with 밝다 bright or 비치다 to shine. A soft 달빛 is described with 은은하다, and 달빛 아래 means under the moonlight.
mistakes: Confusing 달빛 moonlight with 별빛 starlight
Saying 달빛이 와요 instead of 달빛이 비쳐요

examples: Big snowflakes are coming down thickly.
Big snowflakes fell so it is really pretty.
nuance: 함박눈 means large fluffy snowflakes and uses the same verbs as 눈, so you say 함박눈이 와요 or 내려요. The adverb 펑펑 describes it falling thickly. Koreans love 함박눈 because it looks beautiful and piles up fast.
mistakes: Saying 함박눈이 불어요 with the wind verb instead of 함박눈이 와요
Confusing 함박눈 large snowflakes with 진눈깨비 sleet

examples: Dark clouds gathered in the sky.
먹구름이 몰려와서 곧 비가 올 것 같아요.
Dark clouds rolled in so it looks like rain soon.
It is dark because there are many dark clouds.
nuance: 먹구름 is a dark gray rain cloud, combining 먹 ink with 구름 cloud. It pairs with 끼다 to gather or 몰려오다 to roll in and usually warns that rain is coming. When the sky has many 먹구름, it gets dark and gloomy.
mistakes: Saying 먹구름이 와요 like 비가 와요 instead of 먹구름이 껴요
Confusing 먹구름 dark cloud with plain 구름 cloud

examples: The temperature drops a lot at night.
The room temperature is just right.
nuance: 온도 means temperature for the air, water, or a room, while 기온 is specifically the air temperature outside. It pairs with 높다 high and 낮다 low, and 올라가다 or 내려가다 for change. Use 온도 broadly for anything you can measure with a thermometer.
mistakes: Using 온도 for outside weather when 기온 is more precise
Saying 온도가 커요 instead of 온도가 높아요

examples: The temperature drops below zero at night.
This morning is minus five degrees.
nuance: 영하 means below zero degrees and comes before the number, as in 영하 5도 for minus five degrees. Its opposite is 영상 above zero. You hear 영하 a lot in winter weather forecasts in Korea.
mistakes: Putting the number before 영하 as in 5도 영하 instead of 영하 5도
Confusing 영하 below zero with 영상 above zero

examples: The drought is severe this year.
A drought set in because it did not rain.
I save water during a drought.
nuance: 가뭄 is a drought, a long period with little rain, and uses the verb 들다 as in 가뭄이 들다 to set in. It is described with 심하다 severe or 계속되다 to continue. It is the opposite situation from 장마, the rainy season.
mistakes: Saying 가뭄이 와요 instead of the natural 가뭄이 들다
Confusing 가뭄 drought with 장마 the rainy season
